title: Building a Zero-Cloud Speech-to-Text Pipeline
excerpt: Why I built WhisperFlow offline, the whisper.cpp + llama.cpp split, and a stdlib-only Python orchestrator.
content: When building WhisperFlow, I wanted to avoid third-party APIs to keep transcription entirely offline. I decided to use a Python orchestrator to connect whisper.cpp with a local llama.cpp server. The transcription engine calls whisper-cli via subprocesses to output JSON data (-oj), which is parsed to extract segment arrays and millisecond timestamps. By writing the orchestrator using only Python's standard library, I avoided heavy dependencies while still supporting subtitle outputs like SRT and VTT. It runs sub-30-second audio files quickly and securely on consumer hardware, and no audio ever leaves the machine.

title: Synchronous Inputs in a Sandboxed Browser Environment
excerpt: Running real Python in Nexus-AI via Pyodide/WASM — the SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics bridge for synchronous input().
content: In Nexus-AI, running user-written Python code in the browser meant compiling Pyodide into a Web Worker. However, supporting Python's synchronous input() function within the browser's asynchronous architecture presented a challenge. To solve this, I built a shared memory channel using SharedArrayBuffer and Atomics between the main thread and the worker. The worker calls Atomics.wait() on a control array, pausing execution until the user submits text. The Node server uses COOP and COEP headers to enable shared memory access while keeping scripts isolated. A 10-second timeout guard terminates runaway scripts so an infinite loop can't freeze the game.

title: Intercepting Agent Payloads in the MAIN World
excerpt: Why Agent Safety Net needs MAIN world injection — declarativeNetRequest can't see request bodies, so we monkey-patch fetch/XHR.
content: While developing Agent Safety Net, I found that Chrome's Manifest V3 declarativeNetRequest API cannot inspect request bodies. To check outgoing agent prompts for prompt injection, I had to patch the connection interface. I wrote a script that mounts to the page's MAIN execution world and monkey-patches window.fetch and XMLHttpRequest.prototype.open. Outgoing payloads are captured and routed via window.postMessage to an isolated content script, which passes them to a background Service Worker. This three-hop pipeline evaluates prompts for PII and prompt injection in under a millisecond, then surfaces a four-tier intervention UI (allow, warn, confirm, block) based on the verdict.

title: Balancing SQLite and ChromaDB in Local RAG
excerpt: Why 2'nd_Brain uses SQLite + ChromaDB (not one or the other) — and the SSE write-back race I had to solve.
content: For 2'nd_Brain, I designed a hybrid dual-store architecture using SQLite and ChromaDB. SQLite stores conversation records and document metadata, while ChromaDB manages semantic vector indexes. When a user asks a question, the backend queries ChromaDB for relevant text chunks, while SQLite fetches historical facts to build the context. After the LLM streams its answer via Server-Sent Events, a background worker extracts new memories and writes them back to SQLite. Decoupling the write-back from the live stream solved a race condition — the user sees their answer immediately, and memory persistence happens after the stream closes. A /graph endpoint also builds a knowledge graph of document, chunk, and memory nodes connected by keyword-overlap edges.

title: Building StudyOS as a Local GATE Prep PWA
excerpt: A local-first PWA with 13 Prisma models, a test-runner state machine, and a local LLM for answer evaluation — dogfooded daily for GATE 2027.
content: I built StudyOS as a local progressive web app to track my prep for the GATE 2027 exam. Using Next.js 16 and Prisma, I mapped out the exam syllabus into 13 relational tables in SQLite covering subjects, topics, test attempts, study sessions, notes, and documents. The dashboard tracks progress across topics using Recharts, calculating completion rates based on mock exam scores. I integrated a local LLM instance via llama.cpp to evaluate my answers and explain complex questions offline — no API keys, no cloud calls. Drag-and-drop topic prioritization is built with dnd-kit, and the whole app is installable as a PWA with offline support. Serving this setup locally keeps my study data private and easily accessible on the go.
